title: Top Comments: Finding the Source of High Energy Neutrinos

Francis Halzen, a physics professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, won this year’s Nobel Prize in Physics for being the principal creative energy behind the experiment called IceCube, in Antarctica, which was designed to observe high-energy neutrinos. IceCube is an experiment a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice to observe neutrinos.

Neutrinos, of course, are nearly-massless particles that only interact with other particles through what is called the weak nuclear force, which is responsible for beta decay. Because the weak force is so weak, they only rarely interact with other matter, and so they mainly just pass through all matter without any effect. Trillions of neutrinos pass through your body in a day, but you’d never know it. Detection of neutrinos requires detectors featuring large amounts of matter that could, on rare occasion, interact with the neutrino to cause an atom to emit an electron or antielectron, which will produce a detectable flash.

The nuclear fusion that occurs in the Sun’s core, which is what produces the sunlight that powers most of life on Earth, also produces neutrinos, which can then be observed in these neutrino detectors. In principle, solar neutrinos can be used to diagnose what is happening in the core of the Sun at any given time because they are unimpeded as they pass through the matter of the Sun to arrive at Earth at nearly the speed of light. Other radiation produced in the Sun’s core, including light, may take years to make it to the surface, but neutrinos emerge immediately.

However, the IceCube experiment was not designed to detect solar neutrinos. It was designed to detect cosmic neutrinos, that is, neutrinos that emerge from extremely energetic processes that occur well outside the Milky Way Galaxy. Because cosmic neutrinos are produced in extremely energetic processes, the neutrinos observed by IceCube are extremely high-energy, as high as peta electronvolts (peta = 1015). By comparison, solar neutrinos have energies in the range of 17 18 mega electronvolts (mega = 106). Further, IceCube is capable of tracking the direction in which these neutrinos are traveling, so they can be tracked back to their source. For example, a high-energy neutrino detected in 2017 was traced back to a quasar–a very distant cosmic object consisting of a highly active supermassive black hole in the process of tearing matter apart–as the energetic neutrino was detected at the same time that a gamma ray outburst was being observed from that object. However, as I pointed out above, light (such as gamma rays) interact with matter that may lie between the neutrino source and the Earth, so we may miss a gamma ray burst signature associated with an energetic neutrino.

However, looking for high-energy light, such as gamma rays, may not be the best way to look for the source of energetic neutrinos. A new report gives details on looking for their sources using radioastronomy. Energetic cosmic objects also emit copious amounts of radio wave radiation, and this long-wavelength, low energy radiation is much more capable of traveling through the matter in the universe without being absorbed or deflected compared with more energetic radiation.

In 2017, the Very Large Array in New Mexico began tracking how radio emissions from space change in brightness over time, a project known as the Very Large Array Sky Survey, or VLASS for short. My team and I recently showed that most of the objects seen by VLASS with fluctuating radio emissions are quasars, of the same type that IceCube previously saw producing neutrinos.

Interestingly, when we compared the times that IceCube detected neutrinos with the times when objects spotted by VLASS experienced flares of radio emission, there appeared to be a correlation.

Put another way, when an astrophysical neutrino is detected by IceCube, there is a radio source brightening in the same part of the sky, more often than you’d expect from random chance. These radio flares seem to only be associated with about 13% of the astrophysical neutrinos detected by IceCube, which means we still can’t account for the origin of the majority of astrophysical neutrinos. However, more than 90% of the radio outbursts potentially associated with neutrinos aren’t seen at all by our gamma-ray telescopes.

So radioastronomy may be better suited to find the sources of energetic neutrinos than gamma ray astronomy.
